EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT OF THE SECTION

PUBLIC SCHOOLS.—That such a population should readily take advantage of the provisions for public schools included in the Constitution of 1876 was to be expected. A cross-section of public-school development in Fannin County is quoted from Carter's History of Fannin County for this and other counties in the area:

The County Judge, by virtue of his office, is superintendent of the schools of the county, which is an ex officio district school superintendent. The annual apportionment of school funds from the State government to each of these communities is fifty-nine pupils. The apportionment of funds from the State in 1885 is $5.30 to each child of scholastic age, and, by all accounts, these facts are very revealing in their import. The annual apportionment of funds from the State government keeps pace with the increase of pupils, by reason of accrued interest on the continued use and addition to the free school fund.

The number enrolled for the district free schools enrolled for the next term of free schools, which open in September, are 3,706, from which, of course, must be deducted all for free schools. The enrollment of 781 do not know how to read; of the 1,029 colored children, there are 388 who can not read.

All the schools are presided over by competent, and most of them thorough teachers, whose testimonials and certificates from third to first degree are granted, when the applicant shows to the satisfaction of the Board of Examiners that he is well educated, and is not confined to text books, but has attended (and very properly) to the importance of clear methods of imparting knowledge, and to his thorough acquisition of the most improved modes of teaching.
